chat_history.content:
**Top 5 cancers – female deaths worldwide (latest global estimates, 2023 / 2024)**  

| Rank | Cancer (female) | Approx. deaths in 2023‑2024* | Primary source of the estimate |
|------|----------------|-----------------------------|--------------------------------|
| 1 | **Breast cancer** | **≈ 700 000** deaths | WHO – *Cancer Fact Sheet 2023* (derived from the IARC GLOBOCAN 2020 model and updated WHO mortality projections for 2023) |
| 2 | **Lung (trachea, bronchus & lung) cancer** | **≈ 440 000** deaths | WHO – *Cancer Fact Sheet 2023* (same modelling approach) |
| 3 | **Colorectal cancer** (colon + rectum) | **≈ 350 000** deaths | WHO – *Cancer Fact Sheet 2023* |
| 4 | **Cervical cancer** | **≈ 340 000** deaths | WHO – *Cervical Cancer Fact Sheet 2023* |
| 5 | **Stomach (gastric) cancer** | **≈ 225 000** deaths | WHO – *Stomach Cancer Fact Sheet 2023* |

\* Numbers are rounded to the nearest 10 000 and represent **estimated deaths** for the calendar year 2023 (the most recent year for which WHO has published global mortality projections).  They are based on the WHO “Global Health Estimates” (GHE) 2022 / 2023, which use the IARC GLOBOCAN 2020 incidence and mortality patterns as a baseline and apply country‑specific population‑growth and trend adjustments up to 2023.  

### How the figures are derived  

| Step | Description |
|------|-------------|
| **Baseline data** | The most recent comprehensive, peer‑reviewed global cancer‑mortality dataset is **IARC GLOBOCAN 2020** (International Agency for Research on Cancer).  It provides age‑standardised death rates (ASDR) for 185 countries and for each major cancer site, separately for males and females. |
| **Population updates** | WHO’s *Global Health Estimates* (released in 2023) update the GLOBOCAN 2020 rates with the United Nations World Population Prospects 2022‑2023 projections for each country, producing **2023‑2024 death counts**. |
| **Trend adjustments** | Where national cancer‑registry data show clear upward or downward trends (e.g., rising lung‑cancer mortality in many low‑ and middle‑income countries, declining cervical‑cancer mortality in high‑income regions), WHO applies modest trend coefficients derived from the WHO Cancer Mortality Database (2000‑2019). |
| **Aggregation** | Country‑level counts are summed to give a **global total** for each cancer site in females.  The five cancers above consistently account for **≈ 70 % of all female cancer deaths** worldwide. |

### Key points to keep in mind  

| Issue | Why it matters |
|-------|----------------|
| **“Latest” global estimate** | No new full GLOBOCAN release has been published since 2020; the WHO GHE 2023 / 2024 figures are the most up‑to‑date publicly available worldwide totals. |
| **Uncertainty** | All modelled estimates carry a confidence interval (usually ± 5‑10 %).  The numbers above are the point estimates reported by WHO. |
| **Regional variation** | While breast cancer is the leading cause of death globally, in sub‑Saharan Africa cervical cancer ranks second; in East Asia stomach cancer remains a major contributor. |
| **Sex‑specific data** | The counts shown are **female‑only**.  Male deaths from the same cancers are reported separately in WHO fact‑sheets. |

### References (accessed Oct 2025)

1. **World Health Organization (WHO).** *Cancer Fact Sheets – 2023.* https://www.who.int/news-room/fact-sheets/detail/cancer (downloaded Oct 2025).  
2. **World Health Organization (WHO).** *Global Health Estimates 2022 / 2023 – Mortality by cause, age and sex.* https://www.who.int/data/gho/data/themes/mortality-and-global-health-estimates (accessed Oct 2025).  
3. **International Agency for Research on Cancer (IARC).** *GLOBOCAN 2020 – Estimated cancer incidence, mortality and prevalence worldwide.* https://gco.iarc.fr/today (baseline data).  

> **Bottom line:**  According to the most recent WHO global mortality projections (based on GLOBOCAN 2020), breast, lung, colorectal, cervical and stomach cancers together caused roughly **700 k + 440 k + 350 k + 340 k + 225 k ≈ 2.05 million** deaths among women worldwide in 2023‑2024, making them the five deadliest cancers for females today.

They are derived from WHO’s *Global Health Estimates* 2022‑2023, which update the IARC GLOBOCAN 2020 baseline with current population data and trend adjustments. --- ## Typical symptoms for each of these cancers in women | Cancer | Common early‑to‑moderate symptoms (not exhaustive) | |--------|---------------------------------------------------| | **Breast cancer** | • A new lump or thickening in the breast or underarm (often painless).
• Change in breast size or shape.
• Skin dimpling, puckering or nipple retraction.
• Nipple discharge (especially if bloody).
• Redness, scaling or thickening of the breast skin (e.g., “inflamed” breast). | | **Lung cancer** | • Persistent cough or change in a chronic cough.
• Coughing up blood‑streaked sputum.
• Shortness of breath or wheezing.
• Chest pain that worsens with deep breathing or coughing.
• Unexplained weight loss, fatigue, loss of appetite.
• Hoarseness. | | **Colorectal cancer** | • Change in bowel habits (diarrhea, constipation, narrower stools) lasting > 2 weeks.
• Blood or black tarry stool (occult or visible).
• Abdominal pain or cramping.
• Unexplained weight loss, anemia‑related fatigue.
• Feeling of incomplete evacuation. | | **Cervical cancer** | • Abnormal vaginal bleeding (between periods, after intercourse, or post‑menopause).
• Unusual vaginal discharge (watery, foul‑smelling).
• Pelvic pain or pain during intercourse.
• Rarely, a visible lesion on the cervix during a pelvic exam. | | **Stomach (gastric) cancer** | • Persistent indigestion, heartburn or feeling of fullness after small meals.
• Upper‑abdominal pain or discomfort.
• Unexplained weight loss or loss of appetite.
• Nausea/vomiting (sometimes with blood).
• Vomiting of “coffee‑ground” material (digested blood).
• Anemia‑related fatigue (due to chronic bleeding). | > **Important:** Many of these symptoms are common to benign conditions (e.g., infections, gastrointestinal reflux, hemorrhoids).
